_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 7 Networks and the Internet. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (a network; the router; wired and wireless; the internet; when it is not there), in the lesson's own words and with its own things: the kit's internet scene at states 0 and 1 for one computer and two joined, the Network builder's router and its five devices, the Wire spotter's two bins, and the Offline tester's apps.
title: Networks and the Internet
subtitle: Grade 1 Computing
objectives: Know that some devices can connect to each other to make a network.
Know that the internet consists of many computers that are connected together around the world.
Identify that some devices are connected by wires and that other devices are not.
Know that there are times when the internet is not available.

beats.say: Look at one computer, sitting on its own. It cannot send anything anywhere.
Join it to another, and the two of them can share.
Here is one computer, on its own.
It cannot send anything anywhere.
Now take a cable, and join it to another computer.
Straight away they can send each other messages and pictures.
Devices joined together so they can share are called a network.
At home, every device joins the network through one box.
It is called a router, and it has little blinking lights.
The laptop and the printer plug into it with a wire.
The tablet and the phone join with no wire at all.
Now the tablet can send a picture to the printer, through the router.
A wired device has a cable carrying its connection.
A desktop computer with a cable into the wall is wired. So are headphones.
A wireless device connects through the air, with no cable at all.
A tablet is wireless. So is a phone, and so is a smart watch.
Both are connected. You just cannot see the wireless one.
Your home network is one of millions, all around the world.
Join all of those networks together, and you have the internet.
Your home joins it through the router.
So does a school far away. So does Grandma's phone.
Send Grandma a message, and it crosses the whole world in about a second.
The internet is not one big computer. It is millions of them, joined.
Sometimes the internet is not available at all.
On a plane, in a tunnel, or when the router at home breaks.
Switch it off, and try each thing on the tablet.
A video online stops. A video call stops. A message cannot go.
All three need other computers, and they cannot be reached.
Drawing still works. A saved game still works. Your photos still work.
They are already on the tablet, so they need nobody else.
A network is devices joined together so they can share.
At home they join through the router, some with a wire and some with none.
The internet is many computers joined together around the world.
And there are times when it is not there. Then everything else carries on.
